description: ProGarLabs is a technology lab from Osorno, Chile, combining GIS, machine learning, software engineering, UI/UX and product design. We're tackling NASA Space Apps 2026's Earth System Trend Detective challenge to explore NASA data, identify environmental trends and assess their significance. We welcome collaborators in Earth science, remote sensing, climate data, statistics and time-series analysis. Join us to build a scientifically rigorous, open and impactful solution!
summary: Trend Detective Lab turns NASA Earth data into tested evidence about environmental change. On a 3D globe you explore Chile's 16 regions, open NASA trends with their 95 % intervals and p-values, test whether two trends really differ, and read what the evidence can — and cannot — show. It answers the challenge end to end: choose a variable measured by a NASA mission or produced by a NASA model, see its time series, and find out what is changing, where, how fast and how certain it is. Built by ProGarLabs with MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GLDAS and MUR SST, an open reproducible Python pipeline and a public web app. It matters because a regional average can hide opposite changes inside a region, products can disagree, and a trend can depend on the period chosen: the app shows all three instead of a single number.
details: What it does. Detecting a trend is easy; knowing what it means is not. Regional averages hide where change happens, products disagree, results depend on the period chosen, and "significant" is over-read. Trend Detective Lab answers the challenge with three layers. Discovery (Earth Atlas): a CesiumJS globe with Chile's 16 regions coloured by their NASA trends (air temperature, precipitation); native NASA cells clipped to two study territories (Antofagasta, Los Lagos) with 3D relief; the highest and lowest cell trend shown automatically; statistical windows (1980-2025, 1980-2002, 2003-2025); and a colour scale that is either adjusted to the window or fixed across windows, always labelled. A 30-second film rendered from the same engine introduces the case, and a presenter mode runs a guided 4:35 tour inside the live app. Evidence (Research Lab): for any region and variable, the time series; the trend with its 95 % confidence interval, p-value and false-discovery-rate q across 16 regions; a direct test of the difference between two regions; sensitivity to the period; cross-checks against ERA5 and weather stations with their dependencies stated; and evidence cards saying what each result supports and what it does not. Reproducibility: an open Python pipeline (fetch from the NASA Giovanni time-series service, aggregate, test, validate, build the JSON files the app reads), 54 science tests and 37 frontend tests in continuous integration, browser smoke tests, and every number traceable to generated files. Method. Monthly anomalies, yearly means, least-squares slope with a lag-1 effective sample size (chosen and calibrated by simulation; worst simulated false-positive rates 8.6 % at 46 years and 10.1 % at 27 years, disclosed), Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall as robustness checks, Benjamini-Hochberg across 16 regions, and differences tested on the difference series rather than by comparing two p-values. Key findings. (1) Confirmatory, question fixed before the analysis: in MERRA-2, 1980-2025, Antofagasta warmed +0.23 C per decade and Los Lagos +0.05; the difference, tested directly, is +0.18 C per decade (95 % CI +0.05 to +0.31, p = 0.006). (2) Exploratory: inside Antofagasta, coastal cells show -0.03 C per decade and interior cells +0.27 (difference -0.29, p < 0.001) over 1980-2025, but in 2003-2025 both warm (+0.43 and +0.52) and the difference is not significant; coastal sea-surface temperature (NASA MUR, 2003-2025) +0.11 C per decade, not significant. No cause is claimed. (3) Datasets disagree: in Magallanes, IMERG shows a significant precipitation decline (-12.2 mm/month per decade, 1998-2024, p = 0.001, q = 0.02) that neither the Punta Arenas station nor ERA5 reproduces; the app shows the disagreement instead of hiding it. Benefits and impact. It teaches a transferable skill - telling an apparent trend from a supported one - to students, teachers and regional planners (as a first look, not an operational tool). The pipeline is region-agnostic (region polygons plus Giovanni variables), open source under Apache-2.0, and runs as a static web app with no backend. What we considered. Trends only (no causes, no forecasts); reanalysis and land-surface model products are not direct measurements; 25-50 km cells cannot resolve finer terrain; coast and elevation are confounded at that scale; ERA5 and MERRA-2 share observations; exploratory analyses were decided after the main results and are labelled as such. Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, Shapely, pyMannKendall), QGIS and GDAL, React, TypeScript, Vite, CesiumJS, Three.js, Observable Plot, FFmpeg, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. How it is creative. A direct test of the difference between trends; uncertainty and disagreement between sources shown, not hidden; NASA cells drawn on the curved globe and on relief; and the same engine produces the app, the film and the presentation. SI disclosure. Code and documentation were written with SI coding assistants (Anthropic Claude via Claude Code; OpenAI Codex for an independent review) under the team's direction; every statistic comes from our reproducible Python code, not from a language model. The film is a frame-by-frame render of the app (no image or video generator). Its instrumental music was generated with MiniMax Music 3.0 (AI-generated), edited and reviewed by ProGarLabs; this is stated in the video's description and metadata.
